title: Signal direction changed decoding order in ten matched Allen circuit model sets
abstract: We tested whether a mean noise variance rank gives a constant-signal decoding rank in selected Allen slice circuit models. We used 247 mouse VisP and 17 human TCx graph sets. Fixed labeled degrees, class totals, selected motifs and signed spectra left alternatives in ten sets. Every one of their 19 state pairs favored different unit-norm signal directions under optimal full-state Gaussian decoding. Twelve pairs were not equivalent under class-preserving cell permutations. At gain 0.15, the largest snapshot contrast was 0.245099 times the unconnected model information. Coordinate and uniform inputs gave much smaller contrasts. For a 1000-unit stationary average, the largest normalized contrast fell to 0.000247. An exact calculation gives the same limiting information rate for all stable wirings under full observation and fixed positive definite input noise. This rate identity is a linear-filter control, not a new biological law. Independent covariance checks passed. Assumed weights, signed optimized inputs, common decay, full observation, slice sampling and no linked activity data limit biological use. Code, aggregate evidence, provenance and external retrieval instructions support reproduction.

display.caption: Gain 0.15. Left: exact maximum absolute Fisher information contrast over unit-norm signal directions and state pairs in each of ten model sets. Right: two snapshot-optimized signals kept fixed across windows in the prior six-cell witness. Values are divided by unconnected-model information at each window. Time is in assumed common decay units. These are model calculations, not measured decoding effects.

Motivates a direct information test after prior variance sensitivity results.
